subtype: Approach: finding a game they can play together [Thinking]
passage: It had been raining all day, and there was only one game console in the house. Salma and her brother Harsha both wanted the controller. "My turn!" "No, mine!" They were about to start again when Salma stopped and looked at the shelf. "We keep asking whose turn it is," she said. "That's the wrong question. What could the two of us play together?" Harsha blinked. "There's the racing game that has two controllers." They plugged in the second one, sat side by side, and spent the afternoon racing each other around the track, laughing about who crashed into the barrier the most.

qa.q: What kind of game did Harsha and Salma choose?
qa.a: They chose the racing game with two controllers.

qa.q: How did Salma feel about the fight over turns?
qa.a: Salma was frustrated that they kept asking whose turn it was and decided it was the wrong question; she wanted something the two of them could play together.

qa.q: What alternative approach could they use if the two-player game becomes boring, and why?
qa.a: They could use a timer to share turns or choose a board game. Either gives a fair option without a fight.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Salma's new question?
qa.a: Harsha blinked, then found the racing game right away, so Harsha probably felt surprised and happy to swap arguing for playing together.

grounding: Instead of fighting over the game, two siblings choose a two-player game, reframing the problem from whose turn to what they can do together.
